_meta.description: Names and categories deliberately not in the universe. Scope discipline made explicit — an omission recorded here is a decision, not an oversight.

categories.body: Raw materials, energy, critical minerals and the AI/semiconductor chain are mapped end-to-end in the sibling repositories. Including them here would duplicate the research and blur the thesis.

items.n: Critical minerals, mining, energy, grid equipment
items.why: hard-assets-research covers the whole chain. The one genuine overlap is grid contractors — PWR and MYRG appear here for their labour pool, not for their end market.

items.n: Semiconductors, AI hardware, optical, robotics components
items.why: ai-hardware-research covers this end-to-end. The automation names held here (ROK, EMR, Fanuc, Keyence) are held for the labour-substitution argument specifically, and the deeper supply chain behind them lives in the sibling map.

categories.body: Businesses commonly bundled into 'the aging trade' whose actual earnings driver is something else. Including them would let a weak name borrow the thesis's credibility.

items.n: Large-cap diversified pharma (PFE, MRK, JNJ, ABBV)
items.why: Patent cliffs, pipeline outcomes and pricing policy dominate. The demographic signal is real but so diluted it contributes nothing to a position decision.

Volumes do rise with age, but the earnings driver is payor mix, commercial rate negotiation and labour cost. Limb C is a headwind here, not a tailwind — hospitals are on the wrong side of the wage argument.

items.n: Life insurance writers as a group
items.why: Mortality-exposed rather than longevity-exposed, so the demographic effect is the opposite sign to the rest of the thesis. RGA is included specifically because it takes longevity risk professionally on both sides; the group as a whole is not a thesis expression.
Employer-market economics have no demographic content. The pay vertical holds only the Medicare-exposed part of each name's story.

categories.body: Frequently cited in aging-theme lists on the strength of a story rather than a demonstrable earnings driver.

items.why: Speculative science with no revenue linkage to the cohort clock. If it works, it is limb D's falsifier rather than its expression — which is an argument against owning it inside this book.

items.n: Senior-focused consumer apps and social platforms
items.why: No demonstrated monetisation of an older user base at scale. Recurrent as a venture theme, absent as a listed one.

items.n: Medical alert and personal emergency response devices
items.why: Genuine demographic demand, but the category has commoditised and the listed pure plays have mostly been taken private or absorbed. Flagged as a gap in aging-in-place coverage rather than filled with a poor proxy.
FOA is included as the category's dominant originator and as a monitoring instrument. The rest of the category has repeatedly failed to convert unanswerable product logic into a durable business.

categories.body: The demographic exposure is right; the security is not investable in the form available.

items.n: European senior care operators (Clariane, Attendo, Orpea successor entities)
items.why: The demographic exposure is textbook. The sector's governance and quality-of-care scandals, plus heavy leverage against regulated pricing, make it uninvestable on the evidence.
Both run the same clock — China's ahead of the US in speed if not in level. Excluded for now on disclosure quality and policy risk, not on thesis grounds. A genuine future extension of the map.
Creative Planning, Captrust and Mariner are arguably better expressions of limb B than anything listed. Unavailable — their M&A multiples are used as the private mark for the listed comps instead.

Permobil, Stannah and Bruno are the aging-in-place hardware layer and are almost entirely private. Recorded as a coverage gap rather than proxied through LEG, which is a furniture and automotive components business with an adjustable-bed line.

categories.body: Excluded as expressions, tracked as sentiment instruments.

items.why: Holdings are typically large-cap diversified healthcare selected by keyword rather than by demographic gradient — precisely the flattening this dashboard exists to avoid. Useful only as a crowding gauge: flows into these funds are a direct read on how consensus the trade has become.
No demographic selection at all. Held as a benchmark for whether the stock-level work adds anything, not as a position.

coverage_gaps.title: Known holes in v1
coverage_gaps.intro: Stated plainly so the map's edges are visible. Each of these is a place where the thesis has an argument and the universe does not yet have an expression.
gaps: Aging-in-place hardware — mobility, stairlifts, bathroom modification. Almost entirely private. The listed route runs through HD, LOW and IBP, all heavily diluted.
Estate planning technology — the least-penetrated part of limb B and entirely private (Vanilla, Wealth.com, Trust & Will).
Non-US expressions beyond Europe and Japan. China and India run the same clock and are absent.
Fixed income and rates expressions. The thesis has an explicit rate view (weakness w2) and the universe currently contains no instrument for it — everything here is equity.
The median-retiree segment is under-covered relative to its size. It is the largest cohort segment by headcount, the thinnest on crowding, and has only a handful of names against it.
Caregiving burden on the working-age population — the labour-supply effect of family members leaving work to provide care. A real limb C channel with no expression yet identified.
